cycle_length.title: Cycles shorter or longer than usual
cycle_length.noticed: Her last 3 cycles were each shorter than 21 days or longer than the usual range.
cycle_length.why: Cycles that are often very short or very long can be linked to hormone or thyroid changes, stress or other conditions a doctor can check.

irregular.title: Irregular cycles
irregular.noticed: Her recent cycle lengths vary more than is typical for her age.
irregular.why: Very irregular cycles can have many causes, such as PCOS, thyroid changes or stress.

long_period.title: Long periods
long_period.noticed: At least 2 of her last 3 periods lasted more than 7 days.
long_period.why: Bleeding for more than a week can lead to low iron (anaemia) and is worth checking.

missed.title: No period for over 90 days
missed.noticed: No period has been logged for more than 3 months.
missed.why: Missing periods can be caused by pregnancy, weight change, stress, PCOS or thyroid changes.

heavy_flow.title: Very heavy flow
heavy_flow.noticed: Very heavy flow was logged in at least 2 of her last 3 cycles.
heavy_flow.why: Very heavy bleeding can cause anaemia and tiredness. A doctor can help.

severe_pain.title: Severe period pain
severe_pain.noticed: Pain of 8 or more out of 10 was logged in at least 2 of her last 3 cycles.
severe_pain.why: Pain that stops daily life is not something to put up with. Conditions like endometriosis can be treated.

between_bleeding.title: Bleeding between periods
between_bleeding.noticed: Bleeding or spotting was logged between periods in at least 2 of her last 3 cycles.
between_bleeding.why: Bleeding between periods has many causes and is worth checking with a doctor.

missed_log.title: A period may be missing ({{date}})
missed_log.noticed: The cycle starting {{date}} is about twice her usual length, so a period may not have been logged.
missed_log.why: Add the missing period in the calendar so predictions stay accurate.

period_not_ended.title: Period still marked as ongoing
period_not_ended.noticed: The period that started {{date}} has no end day yet.
period_not_ended.why: Set its last day so predictions stay accurate.

what.title: What Ritu stores
what.body: The names, birth years, periods, symptoms, moods, notes, body records (like temperature, sleep, water, weight, pill and due date) and settings you enter. Nothing else. Ritu has no account and collects no device IDs, location or contacts.

where.title: Where it is stored
where.body: Only on this phone, inside the app. Ritu has no server. It works without internet and never sends your data anywhere.

share.title: Sharing
share.body: Ritu shares nothing. There are no ads, no analytics and no crash reporting. Data leaves the phone only when you export a file or a doctor report yourself.

pin.title: PINs
pin.body: A PIN is stored on this phone as a salted hash, never as the PIN itself. Locked profiles show only a name and a lock.

notify.title: Reminders
notify.body: Reminders are scheduled on the phone. By default they say only "Reminder – Tap to open".

export.title: Export and backup
export.body: You can export each profile as CSV and JSON, or save a backup file. Keep these files safe: anyone with the file can read it.

delete.title: Deleting data
delete.body: Delete a profile in its settings, or uninstall the app to delete everything. Deleted data cannot be recovered.

children.title: Children
children.body: A parent or guardian can create a profile for a child under 18. Fertile days are hidden by default and private notes are turned off for these profiles.

medical.title: Not medical advice
medical.body: Predictions are estimates, not medical advice and not birth control. Ritu never diagnoses; it only suggests when it may be worth seeing a doctor.

contact.title: Questions
contact.body: Ask the person or organisation that gave you this app, or the developer listed on the app store page.

ttc.title: Fertility today
ttc.levelHint_peak: The day of ovulation and the 1–2 days before it are the most fertile.
ttc.levelHint_high: Sex every 1–2 days in the fertile days gives the best chance.
ttc.levelHint_low: Pregnancy is less likely outside the fertile days, but not impossible.
ttc.fertilityOff: Fertile days are hidden for this profile. Turn them on in profile settings.
ttc.noPeriods: Log a period to see the fertile days.
ttc.lhPositive: Positive LH test: ovulation often follows within 12–36 hours.
ttc.shift: The temperature rose from {{date}}. This usually means ovulation has already happened.
ttc.chartEmpty: Log the morning temperature for a few days to see a chart here.
ttc.axis: Across: day of the cycle. Up: °C
ttc.note: Temperature shows ovulation only after it happens. If there is no pregnancy after 12 months of trying (6 months if she is 35 or older), see a doctor.

menstrual.1: A hot-water bottle on the lower belly and light walking can ease cramps.
menstrual.2: Change pads every 4–6 hours, or sooner if the flow is heavy, to prevent rashes and infection.
menstrual.3: Iron-rich foods like green leafy vegetables, chana, rajma and jaggery help replace iron lost in bleeding.
menstrual.4: Pain that stops daily work, or soaking a pad every 1–2 hours, is worth showing to a doctor.
menstrual.5: Drink enough water and rest well; it is normal to feel more tired on the first days.

follicular.1: Energy often rises after the period ends: a good time for exercise she enjoys.
follicular.2: Protein at every meal (dal, paneer, eggs, curd) helps keep energy steady.
follicular.3: Some light spotting between periods can happen, but bleeding between periods again and again needs a check-up.
follicular.4: Regular sleep at the same time each night helps keep cycles steady.
follicular.5: Logging symptoms now makes it easier to see which days of the cycle feel best.

ovulation.1: A little pain on one side of the lower belly around ovulation is common and usually settles in a day.
ovulation.2: Clear, stretchy discharge like raw egg white is a sign of the fertile days.
ovulation.3: Fertile-day predictions are estimates and are not a safe way to avoid pregnancy.
ovulation.4: Body temperature rises slightly after ovulation and stays up until the next period.

luteal.1: Bloating, sore breasts or mood changes before a period are common. Less salt and more water can help.
luteal.2: Cravings are normal; roasted chana, fruit or nuts are better than a lot of sweets.
luteal.3: Gentle exercise like walking or yoga can ease PMS.
luteal.4: If mood changes before periods are very strong and affect daily life, talk to a doctor. Help is available.
luteal.5: Keep pads ready: the next period is coming in the next days.

late.1: Stress, illness, travel and weight change can delay a period by some days.
late.2: If there is any chance of pregnancy, a home pregnancy test works from the day the period is due.
late.3: If periods stop for 3 months or more without pregnancy, see a doctor.

trimester1.1: Take folic acid and iron every day as the doctor advises.
trimester1.2: Nausea is common. Small, frequent meals and dry snacks in the morning can help.
trimester1.3: Bleeding, severe belly pain or fainting need a doctor at once.
trimester1.4: Register the pregnancy early at the hospital or with the ANM so check-ups and vaccines are not missed.

trimester2.1: Most women feel the baby move between 18 and 22 weeks.
trimester2.2: Eat a little more: dal, milk, curd, green vegetables and fruit every day.
trimester2.3: Sleeping on the left side helps blood flow to the baby.
trimester2.4: Swelling of the face or hands, bad headache or blurred vision need a doctor at once.

trimester3.1: Notice the baby’s movements every day. If they become fewer, go to the hospital the same day.
trimester3.2: Keep the hospital bag, reports and ID ready from 36 weeks.
trimester3.3: Water leaking, bleeding or regular painful tightening means go to the hospital.
trimester3.4: Plan with the family how to reach the hospital quickly, day or night.
